pending.note: Single best answer

pending.q: A 63‑year‑old woman with chronic renal failure (eGFR 30 mL/min) develops joint pain. Synovial fluid WBC is 45,000/mm³, crystals are absent on microscopy, but Gram stain is negative. Which investigation is the best next step to rule out septic arthritis?
o: Synovial fluid cultures on enriched media for 5 days
pending.e: In patients where crystals are absent but suspicion of septic arthritis remains, synovial fluid culture on enriched media for 5 days provides the gold standard diagnostic yield.
pending.note: Correct and strictly factual

pending.q: In calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (pseudogout) the crystals are best described as:
o: Needle‑shaped, strongly negatively birefringent, yellow when parallel
Rhomboid/rod‑shaped, weakly positively birefringent, blue when parallel
Tiny clumps, non‑birefringent, stain with alizarin red S
Flat plates, not birefringent, seen only in electron microscopy
pending.e: CPPD crystals are rhomboid or rod‑shaped, weakly positively birefringent and appear blue when aligned parallel to the compensator axis.
pending.note: Standard textbook description

pending.q: A 48‑year‑old man with intermittent ankle pain is found to have chronic tophaceous gout. Which skeletal finding is most characteristic on plain radiograph of the affected joint?
o: Joint space narrowing with peri‑articular osteopenia
Destructive punched‑out erosions with sclerotic margins and overhanging edges
Bilateral symmetrical erosions of carpal joints
Uniform subchondral cysts with no erosions
pending.e: Chronic gout produces classic “punched‑out” juxta‑articular erosions with sclerotic margins and overhanging edges (Martel sign).
pending.note: Accurate radiological hallmark

pending.q: A patient with acute pseudogout is being managed. Which of the following is true regarding the crystal morphology seen on polarised light microscopy?
o: They appear yellow when the crystal axis is perpendicular to the compensator
They are not seen by polarised light
pending.e: CPPD crystals are weakly positively birefringent and appear blue when parallel to the compensator; they are rhomboid, not yellow or bipyramidal.
pending.note: Consensus from classic references

pending.q: A 70‑year‑old man with comorbid chronic kidney disease is started on allopurinol for intermittent gout flares. Which of the following precautions is appropriate?
o: Never reduce dose regardless of kidney function
Discontinue allopurinol during an acute flare
Start colchicine concurrently during the first week
Avoid starting in the presence of significant renal impairment and adjust dose
pending.e: Allopurinol dose must be reduced in renal impairment; initiation during a flare is allowed with anti‑inflammatory cover, but dose adjustment is essential.
pending.note: Aligned with guideline and notes

pending.q: Which imaging modality is recommended for mapping the extent of polyostotic Paget disease at diagnosis?
o: Plain radiographs of all affected bones
pending.e: A whole‑body bone scan with 99mTc‑MDP shows intense uptake in all affected bones and is the gold standard for extent mapping.
pending.note: Matches standard guidelines.

pending.q: A 62‑year‑old man with a history of Paget disease of bone presents with new, severe thigh pain and a palpable hard swelling. Radiographs show a lytic lesion with a soft‑tissue mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pending.e: Paget sarcoma (osteosarcoma arising in pagetic bone) is a rare but recognized complication, presenting with a new lytic bone lesion and soft‑tissue mass.
pending.note: Consistent with reference facts.

pending.q: A 42‑year‑old male presents with insidious groin pain worsening on weight‑bearing. Plain film shows no abnormalities. Which investigation is most likely to detect early disease?
pending.e: MRI is the most sensitive and specific test for pre‑radiographic osteonecrosis and can screen the contralateral hip.
pending.note: Direct match to Campbell’s statement on MRI being best for early detection.

pending.q: A 27‑year‑old female with SLE on long‑term methylprednisolone presents with sudden hip pain after a delay of 8 hours in reducing a traumatic dislocation. Which factor most increases her risk of avascular necrosis?
pending.e: Reduction delayed beyond 6 hours after hip dislocation markedly increases the risk of femoral head AVN.
pending.note: Consistent with known pathophysiology of hip dislocation.

pending.q: Which radiographic sign on frog‑leg lateral view is the most ominous predictor of impending femoral head collapse?
pending.e: The crescent sign represents a subchondral fracture and predicts collapse.
pending.note: Reflected in the reference teaching.

pending.q: A 55‑year‑old man with haemoglobin SS disease has bilateral femoral head osteonecrosis. What is the most likely pathophysiological mechanism?
pending.e: In sickle cell disease, microvascular occlusion by sickled cells leads to avascular necrosis.
pending.note: Standard pathogenesis for sickle cell osteonecrosis.

pending.q: In mature cortical bone, type I collagen constitutes approximately what proportion of the organic matrix?
pending.e: Type I collagen accounts for ~90 % of the organic (osteoid) matrix.
pending.note: Spelling‑correct, single best answer, distractors are plausible but incorrect.

pending.q: The degradation products of collagen cross‑links pyridinoline and deoxypyridinoline are best used as markers of which bone process?
pending.e: They are released during collagen breakdown, reflecting bone resorption.
pending.note: Question is clear and the distractors refer to unrelated processes.

pending.q: After a bone cell begins hydroxyapatite deposition, approximately how long does the mineralisation lag last before crystals are detectable?
pending.e: Mineralisation lag is about 10–15 days; longer lag leads to osteomalacia.
pending.note: Each option is a realistic timeframe, but only 10‑15 days matches the physiology.

pending.q: Mutations in which transcription factor are the cause of cleidocranial dysplasia?
pending.e: RUNX2 (CBFA1) is the master regulator of osteoblast differentiation; its loss causes cleidocranial dysplasia.
pending.note: The stem directly asks for the causative gene; answer is unique.

pending.q: Loss‑of‑function mutations in LRP5 lead to which clinical phenotype?
pending.e: LRP5 loss causes osteoporosis‑pseudoglioma syndrome; gain‑of‑function produces high bone mass.
pending.note: Clear distinction between loss and gain of function; distractors are plausible but incorrect.

pending.q: Which osteocyte‑derived protein acts as a systemic inhibitor of bone formation by antagonising Wnt signalling?
pending.e: Sclerostin, produced by osteocytes, binds LRP5/6 and blocks Wnt/β‑catenin, inhibiting osteoblast activity.
pending.note: Only sclerostin directly antagonises Wnt signalling.

pending.q: Which cell is the principal source of RANKL in normal bone remodeling?
pending.e: Osteoblasts and osteocytes secrete RANKL, driving osteoclast differentiation and activation.
pending.note: Distractors represent potential but incorrect sources.

pending.q: The bone‑specific form of alkaline phosphatase (ALP) is best used as a marker of which process?
pending.e: Bone‑specific ALP hydrolyses pyrophosphate and is a marker of osteoblastic bone formation activity.
pending.note: The option aligns with the known function of bone ALP.

pending.q: During a joint arthroscopy, the surgeon notes a faint brown line at the interface of uncalcified and calcified cartilage. Which anatomical structure does this line represent?
pending.e: The tidemark is the basophilic line marking the transition from uncalcified to calcified cartilage.
pending.note: Standard histology fact.

pending.q: A patient undergoes a microfracture procedure for a full‑thickness cartilage defect. To maximise the chance of reparative tissue filling the defect, the surgeon should:
o: Use a drill bit 2.5 mm in diameter
Ensure the fracture holes reach the subchondral bone plate
Create a bevelled entry into the subchondral bone
Avoid penetration of the calcified cartilage layer
pending.e: Effective marrow stimulation requires the fracture holes to penetrate the calcified cartilage and reach subchondral bone so that marrow cells can migrate into the defect.
pending.note: Procedure detail.

pending.q: Which matrix protein is secreted by superficial zone chondrocytes and acts as a boundary lubricant for articular cartilage?
pending.e: Lubricin, or PRG4, is produced by superficial zone chondrocytes and synoviocytes and maintains boundary lubrication of articular surfaces.
pending.note: Clear textbook fact.

pending.q: In late‑stage osteoarthritis, which of the following histological features is most frequently observed in the deep zone of articular cartilage?
o: Pericellular accumulation of type VI collagen
Pericellular thinning of type VI collagen
pending.e: Early‑stage OA shows increased pericellular type VI collagen; its early accumulation, especially in the deep zone, is a hallmark of the disease.
pending.note: Well‑documented OA change.
